newsitem.title: USA: O.J. Simpson's incredible reversal of fortune.
newsitem.headline: O.J. Simpson's incredible reversal of fortune.

text.p: In a stunning reversal of fortune, O.J. Simpson has gone from American football hero to a man found responsible for the brutal murders of his ex-wife and her friend.

Simpson faces no jail time -- he was acquitted of the double murders by a criminal court jury in October 1995 -- but following the Tuesday unanimous decision by the civil court panel he could lose much of what remains of the fortune he built during his playing days and as a TV personality and actor.
His wealth reportedly dwindled to $3 million from the $10.8 million he had at the time of his 1992 divorce from Nicole Brown Simpson.

No Hollywood screenwriter could have made up the twists and turns that led Simpson to where he stands today. His is a rags-to-riches story that captured the attention of America and, since his arrest on June 17, 1994, on the criminal charges, much of the rest of the world.
The appropriate adjective for Simpson has always been "first." He pioneered the multi-million-dollar television endorsements that have since become commonplace for athletes.

He was the first-round pick in the 1969 National Football League draft after leading the University of Southern California to a national championship in 1968 and collecting the coveted Heisman Trophy along the way. In 1973, playing with the Buffalo Bills, he set records running with the ball.

Orenthal James Simpson was born in one of San Francisco's roughest neighbourhoods, the Potrero Hill housing projects, on July 9, 1947. As a youngster he suffered from rickets, a Vitamin D and calcium deficiency and had to wear leg braces. He recovered from the disease but it left him bowlegged.

His mother Eunice toiled long hours as a hospital technician while his father Jimmy Lee Simpson worked as a bank custodian during the day and as a porter in a private club at night. When Simpson was 5 his parents divorced and Eunice was left to raise him and his three siblings.
Simpson spent his teen years as a gang leader, fighting in the streets and engaging in petty crime.
"I was somebody who didn't care about anything," he once told The Los Angeles Times, "and the best thing you can say about me and trouble was that I was borderline."

Simpson credits baseball great Willie Mays with turning his life around after Simpson spent a weekend in a youth detention centre when he was 16. On his release from custody, Simpson received a surprise visit from Mays, his idol, who sometimes helped troubled youngsters.

He enrolled at San Francisco City College and then the University of California two years later. In 1969 he started his career with the the Bills that led to his induction in the football Hall of Fame in 1985.

Simpson married his high school sweetheart, Marquerite Whitley, in 1967, and they had three children. They split up in 1977 and divorced in 1979. Simpson met second wife, Nicole Brown, in June 1977 when she was working at a popular Los Angeles night spot. He was about to turn 30, she was 18.
They married in 1985 after living together for eight years and stayed married for seven more years until their divorce.

In legal terms Simpson was found liable for the death of Ronald Goldman in a lawsuit brought by the victim's family and for the attack on his ex-wife which led to her death. Simpson was sued by his ex-wife's estate but under California law an estate cannot claim wrongful death.
But in the court of public opinion, the verdicts rendered Tuesday amount to the same thing: Simpson murdered both individuals on June 12, 1994.

Nevertheless, during the civil trial Simpson was successful in another court when a judge awarded him the custody of his two children Sydney and Justin, by his marriage to Nicole Brown Simpson. He had voluntarily handed over custody to his ex-wife's family after his arrest.

During Simpson's murder trial and the civil court proceedings, which presiding Judge Hiroshi Fujiosaki described to jurors as a "civil murder trial," he was described by prosecutors and plaintiffs' attorneys as a brooding, jealous man with a fierce temper.
Many people found that hard to reconcile with his public persona of a talented athlete and a poised, courteous celebrity who modestly understated his achievements.
Simpson's image was carefully nurtured after his football career when he stepped into the broadcasting booth as an NFL commentator and acted in about a dozen Hollywood movies.

But his career and his image took a nosedive after his arrest in 1994. He spent more than 15 months in jail before his acquittal. In between trials he sought to regain favour with a distrusting public, many of whom believed he literally got away with murder. He courted the black community, joined a Los Angeles church and made public speeches.
